articles.title: Fast-Tracked Ethnicity: How Genetic Ancestry Test Results Influence the Legitimacy of Identifying with an Ethnic Group
articles.authors: Danielle Gaucher, Justin P. Friesen, Josiane Côté, Janessa Domaradzki, Emma Toews
articles.abstract: Millions of people worldwide have taken genetic ancestry tests, yet their impact on intergroup attitudes remains underexamined. This research examines how genetic ancestry information shapes outgroup members’ perceptions of the legitimacy of ethnic identification. Across three experiments, we predicted that learning about someone’s background through a commercial genetic ancestry test would strengthen the perceived validity of their ethnic affiliation. Study 1 showed that an individual whose identity claim was grounded in genetic test results was viewed as legitimately connected to an ethnic group as one with clear genealogical ties. Study 2 found that an individual claiming genetic testing evidence was also seen as equally eligible for a group-specific scholarship. Study 3 replicated these results, demonstrating that when a person’s eligibility for a representative role was questioned, a genetic testing-based explanation was considered as convincing as genealogical ties. Overall, genetic ancestry tests appear to fast-track outgroup judgments of group membership legitimacy.

articles.title: Toward a Deeper Understanding of Microaggressions: A Review and Roadmap of Perceptions and Perpetration
articles.authors: Lara Bellotti, Sara Zaniboni
articles.abstract: Microaggressions are subtle forms of discrimination that convey derogatory or negative messages toward individuals based on their group membership. In this review, we integrated and critically examined measures of perceived and perpetrated microaggressions ( n = 83) and their associated nomological network from empirical studies ( k = 198). Key findings showed that empirical efforts have predominantly focused on individual-level outcomes and largely neglected antecedents and the co-construction dynamics across roles. After synthetizing the literature, we conclude discussing microaggressions and discrimination literature and outline a roadmap offering recommendations for theoretical and empirical advancements. With this roadmap, we organized the identified blind spots while outlining testable pathways bringing together perpetrators, targets, and bystanders, as well as distal and proximal antecedents. We propose methodological recommendations to support scholars in the development of future research.

articles.title: Do Organizational Researchers Report Their Priors? Reporting Guidelines for Bayesian Methods
articles.authors: Lau Holgersen
articles.abstract: Bayesian methods are increasingly used in management and organizational research, yet the prior distributions on which they depend are often poorly reported. A systematic review of 89 empirical Bayesian studies across 15 leading journals (2001–2025) finds that more than a third do not disclose specific prior distributions and only half of those that mention priors justify their specific choices. In response, we offer seven reporting guidelines for authors, reviewers, and editors that span the specification, justification, and evaluation of priors, organized as a guide from considering Bayesian methods through to reporting priors. Each is grounded in a gap this review documents or in an established methodological practice. As Bayesian adoption broadens in this field, these checkpoints offer a minimum standard for ensuring that prior assumptions remain visible and evaluable.

articles.title: Drinking and the Good Life: A Daily Diary Study
articles.authors: Hannah R. Hamilton, Nicholas R. Buttrick, Shigehiro Oishi
articles.abstract: Given the prevalence of social drinking among college students, understanding the association between social drinking and the good life is key to understanding how students are achieving a good life. This 14-day diary study of undergraduate drinkers ( N = 287) examined whether consuming alcohol with others (vs. alone) and time interacting with romantic partners and friends are associated with satisfaction, meaning in life, and psychological richness. Multilevel modeling suggests social drinking was associated with greater happiness, meaning, and richness that evening. Time with a romantic partner was associated with greater meaning and richness that evening, and time with casual friends was associated with richness. Multilevel structural equation modeling revealed that increases in self-expansion and belongingness and decreases in loneliness partially mediated associations between social drinking and the good life. These results suggest ways in which college students’ social (but not solitary) drinking may help students connect with others and enhance their evening.

articles.title: Paternalistic Helping Toward Older Adults: Essentialist Beliefs About Aging as a Cognitive Basis and Potential Interventions
articles.authors: Zizhuo Chen, Minfan Zhu, Min Xu, Yichao Lv, Shufei Yin, Xin Zhang
articles.abstract: Paternalistic helping can undermine older adults’ autonomy. We investigated essentialist beliefs about aging (EBA), beliefs that age-related changes are inevitable and difficult to modify, as one cognitive basis. Study 1 analyzed 123,127 archival welfare projects, finding stronger essentialist and paternalistic framing in helping projects targeting older adults than in those targeting other age groups. Study 2 ( N = 239) found that EBA were associated with preferences for paternalistic helping. Study 3 ( N = 237) showed experimentally weakening EBA reduced these preferences. Two potential broader interventions complemented this age-specific manipulation. In Study 4 ( N = 231), social constructionist thinking reduced preferences for paternalistic helping through weaker EBA. In Study 5 ( N = 240), inducing awe yielded serial indirect effects through lower need for closure and weaker EBA relative to a neutral control condition, but not a positive emotion condition. The findings supported that EBA may foster paternalism and identified potential interventions.

articles.title: Speaking From the Self: How State Authenticity Increases Subjective Agency and Challenging Voice
articles.authors: Min Ju Lee, Maryam Kouchaki, Andrew Brodsky
articles.abstract: People often avoid speaking up not because they lack ideas, but because voice feels socially risky. We examine whether and how state authenticity—the feeling of alignment with one’s true self—influences challenging voice. Across five experimental studies (four preregistered) spanning field and laboratory samples ( N = 2,195), we manipulate state authenticity and test its relationship with challenging voice. Findings suggest that state authenticity can facilitate challenging voice, with effects emerging either directly or indirectly through increased subjective agency. The agency pathway remained evident when self-presentational concern was modeled simultaneously (Study 3b) and was stronger among individuals lower in extraversion, higher in agreeableness, and higher in dispositional authenticity (Study 4). Drawing on self-determination and self-transcendence perspectives, we argue that authentic states can shift regulation toward internally endorsed action, helping individuals act on their convictions despite interpersonal risk. These findings clarify how and for whom authenticity translates into challenging interpersonal communication.

articles.title: The Existential Function of Spiritual Yearning
articles.authors: Daryl R. Van Tongeren, Patty Van Cappellen, Joshua A. Wilt, Julie J. Exline
articles.abstract: Humans seek to address existential concerns and strive for equanimity in light of potential threats. Across the (non)religious spectrum, people long for existential comfort and satisfaction—namely, they experience spiritual yearning. Across five studies (i.e., four experiments, one longitudinal study; N = 5,791), we examined the existential functions of spiritual yearning. Studies 1 to 3 ( n = 462, n = 922, n = 988) revealed that threats to meaning led to greater reported spiritual yearning to the degree people felt existentially insecure. Study 4 ( n = 424) demonstrated longitudinally how spiritual yearning was affected by the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election. To clarify inconsistent small effects, an internal mini-meta-analysis revealed a modest yet significant effect of existential threats on spiritual yearning. Study 5 ( n = 2,995) provided evidence that fulfilled spiritual yearnings enhance existential security, whereas unfulfilled yearnings undermine security. Spiritual yearning may serve existential functions.

articles.title: Surprise Resets the Mind: An Adaptive Online Reset in Working Memory Selection
articles.authors: Jiahan Yu, Jiewei Zheng, Yingtao Fu, Ning Tang, Bin Li, Jifan Zhou, Mowei Shen, Hui Chen
articles.abstract: Human cognition rapidly adapts to unexpected events in dynamic environments, but it remains unclear whether expectation violations rapidly influence the selection of attended information into working memory. Using the attribute-amnesia paradigm, we introduced expectation violations during the surprise trial to test whether unexpected changes improve reporting of a target feature that had been attended and used but was normally not reported. Across six experiments (total N = 250 college students, aged 17–27 years; 149 females), expectation violations reliably improved surprise-trial report of this feature, indicating greater availability in working memory. This effect occurred not only when the violation concerned the target, but also when it involved broader contextual or auditory changes, suggesting that the effect cannot be characterized simply as enhanced visual attention to the target. These findings suggest that expectation violations trigger a rapid, flexible adjustment of working-memory selection, highlighting its role in dynamically managing information under uncertainty.

articles.title: Grit, Big Five Traits, and Perceived Relevance of Tertiary Music Education on Self-Appraised Career Readiness Among Music-Major Students and Working Graduates
articles.authors: Hao Yi Ho, Yu Guo Wang, Xiao Xi Tee, I Ta Wang, Fung Ying Loo
articles.abstract: This study examined the impacts of grit, Big Five personality traits, and perceived relevance of tertiary music education (PRTME) on self-appraised career readiness (SACR) among music-major students and working graduates. A total of 510 students and 250 working graduates from tertiary music education institutions in Malaysia and China voluntarily participated in the online survey. Using structural equation modeling, 63.2% of the variance in SACR was accounted for among students and 58.7% among working graduates. Following psychometric validation of the newly developed scales, PRTME significantly predicted SACR overall. For grit, only perseverance of effort (PE), but not consistency of interests, predicted SACR overall and PRTME among students. PRTME mediated the effects of agreeableness and PE on SACR in students, but not in working graduates, whereas PE mediated the effects of conscientiousness and open-mindedness on SACR overall. Significant differences were found between students and working graduates and between Malaysian and Chinese samples across several constructs, with interaction effects suggesting that these differences varied across regions. Adjusted structural models were subsequently specified to refine the significant pathways. The findings highlight the value of cultivating personality and career-relevant attributes within tertiary music education institutions to effectively enhance music-major students’ readiness for professional music careers.

articles.title: Coping and Resilience Among Conservatoire Music Students in the United Kingdom: A Survey Study
articles.authors: Frederick Lam, Aaron Williamon
articles.abstract: Musicians face distinct psychological and physical pressures associated with intensive training and professional uncertainty, making coping and resilience key areas of concern for their wellbeing. This study examined how coping strategies and psychological resilience contribute to the health and wellbeing of conservatoire music students in the United Kingdom. One hundred and twenty undergraduate and postgraduate music students from seven U.K. conservatoires completed an online survey measuring coping (selected subscales from the COPE Inventory), psychological resilience (10-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale), general health (36-item Short-Form Health Survey) and wellbeing (Short Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale). Conservatoire music students scored positive reinterpretation and growth as the highest-scoring coping strategy. Resilience scores were lower than comparable population norms; however, interpretation should consider contextual differences between conservatoire training environments and broader adult samples. Coping and resilience were positively correlated; particularly, positive reinterpretation and growth and active coping showed strong correlations with resilience. Furthermore, coping and resilience were positively correlated with wellbeing, whereas health also showed positive associations with resilience and wellbeing. These findings highlight the interconnected roles of coping and resilience in supporting conservatoire music students’ health and wellbeing. Further research is needed to examine factors that influence coping and resilience throughout musicians’ training and inform the development of effective health and wellbeing support systems.

articles.title: Electronic Elements Mitigate AI Composer Bias in Traditional Chinese Folk Music
articles.authors: Peng Qian, Minqi Lyu, Jianping Huang
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly expanding into creative domains; however, audiences often devalue music labeled as AI-composed, a phenomenon known as AI composer bias. This bias can be understood as a mismatch between the low experiential capacity attributed to AI’s mind and the high emotional demands of art. This study examines whether such AI composer bias manifests in traditional Chinese folk music, where yijing (emotional depth and spiritual atmosphere) is central, and tests whether incorporating electronic elements can mitigate it. Using a 2 (music type: traditional folk vs. electronic folk) × 2 (label type: human vs. AI) between-subjects design ( N = 174), we found a strong AI composer bias for traditional Chinese folk music, which disappeared when electronic elements were introduced. The results suggest that electronic elements act as bottom-up cues that enhance schema congruency between acoustic features and the AI composer label. The study not only extends bias research to a non-Western context but also proposes a practical, production-based strategy to mitigate bias, offering implications for the acceptance of AI within culturally significant genres.

articles.title: Perceived Usability of Music-Genre Labels in Musical-Taste Research
articles.authors: Romain Brisson, Renzo Bianchi
articles.abstract: Quantitative research on musical tastes has largely relied on genre-based analyses. However, evidence regarding the usability of such labels is lacking. In the present study, we assessed the extent to which individuals feel able to describe their musical tastes using music-genre labels. Our study was conducted as part of the Étude Longitudinale par Internet Pour les Sciences Sociales , a nationwide research project conducted in France. A total of 1,721 participants (51.5% female) were asked to evaluate the usability of music-genre labels. Results showed that a majority of respondents were uncomfortable with the use of music-genre labels, irrespective of their education, income, and sex. Age was associated with the assessment of music-genre labels, with older people reporting the greatest difficulty using such labels. Overall, our findings suggest that reliance on music-genre labels in research on musical preferences may raise usability and validity concerns.

articles.title: The Spanish Adaptation and Validation of the Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index
articles.authors: Carmen Machuca-Ramos, Juan Lupiáñez, Rafael Román-Caballero
articles.abstract: The Goldsmiths Musical Sophistication Index (Gold-MSI) measures a wide range of musical skills and behaviors in the general adult population, regardless of formal training or musical expertise. Although the inventory has been translated and validated in multiple languages, a Spanish version is lacking. This study presents the Spanish adaptation and validation of the Gold-MSI, based on a preregistered protocol and a sample of 539 Spanish-speaking adults. Participants completed the translated inventory alongside sociodemographic and personality measures, with a subsample ( n = 250) completing a retest. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original bifactor structure, with fit indices closely matching previous validations. Internal consistency (α ~ .80) and test–retest reliability ( r ~ .85) were high for most subscales and the general factor. The Gold-MSI effectively distinguished individuals with extensive musical training and expertise from those with limited or no training. Musical sophistication was positively associated with openness to experience, extraversion, and, among younger participants, with family socioeconomic status. The Spanish Gold-MSI demonstrated strong psychometric properties, supporting its use in Spanish-speaking populations and enabling future cross-cultural research on musical behavior.
